## Welcome to your practice report

This is a **Quarto** document. It mixes ordinary writing with live code, so your
report and your analysis always stay in sync. When you click **Render**, Quarto
runs the code below and builds a finished HTML page.

Try it now: change `author: "Humnah Rashid"` in the header above to your own name,
then click **Render**.

## A first look at the data

The code chunk below reads a small practice dataset from the `data/` folder and
shows the first few rows.

```{r}
patients <- read.csv("data/patients.csv")
head(patients)
```

## A first chart

```{r}
hist(patients$age,
     main = "Age distribution of practice patients",
     xlab = "Age (years)",
     col  = "steelblue")
```

## Your turn

- Most patients are concentrated in the middle age ranges, with fewer patients at the youngest and oldest ages.
- Render again and check that both your sentence and the chart appear.

When you are happy with the result, **commit and sync** your work (the Week 2
course page walks you through this), then submit your repository link on Canvas.

## Patient Statistics
```{r}
nrow(patients)
max(patients$age, na.rm = TRUE)
min(patients$age, na.rm = TRUE)
mean(patients$age, na.rm = TRUE)
```

## My Notes

- I learned how the different parts of a Quarto file fit together and how rendering turns the source file into the final HTML report. **I also feel a lot more comfortable with the basic GitHub workflow now, especially saving changes, committing them, and syncing them back to my repository.**

- AI helped me understand some of the course terminology, and I verified the changes by rendering the report and checking the updated HTML myself.
